assertions.notes: The answer explains that without bracketed paste, pasted text arrives like typing and pasted newlines come through as Enter key events that trigger execution. It names the ESC[200~ wrapper rather than mode 2004, but the mechanism is the same.
The code calls execute!(stdout(), EnableBracketedPaste) and handles Event::Paste(String), and the answer says Ratatui/Crossterm do not enable bracketed paste by default.

The answer chooses to reject multiline pastes with a visible message, compares this with keeping the first line or using a multiline editor, and states that paste must never execute, with a test that a multiline paste runs zero commands.
The answer says to disable paste mode on normal exit, errors, panic cleanup, and shell handoff, and warns against assuming ratatui::restore() cleans up modes you enabled yourself.
The answer says pasted newlines arrive as Enter key events, and notes that without bracketed paste (the ESC[200~/201~ wrapping) typed and pasted input can't be told apart.
It enables EnableBracketedPaste via crossterm, handles Event::Paste(String), and says bracketed paste is opt-in with Crossterm; Ratatui only renders and leaves input to the event loop.
It explicitly chooses to reject multiline pastes with a visible message, offers a multiline editor as the alternative, and comments that the paste branch never executes.
It disables the mode on normal exit, errors, panics, suspend and handoff, and states that Ratatui's default restoration does not clean up this extra mode.
Says paste arrives as ordinary keystrokes so each pasted newline becomes Enter and runs the buffer, and that without bracketed-paste support pasted newlines and typed Enter are indistinguishable.

Shows execute!(stdout(), EnableBracketedPaste) and handles Event::Paste, but never clearly says that crossterm and Ratatui leave bracketed paste off by default; it only says Ratatui 'doesn't protect your input handling automatically'.
Recommends rejecting the whole multi-line paste and leaving the buffer unchanged, mentions keeping the first line as an alternative, and states that a paste causes no execution or submit.
Pairs setup with DisableBracketedPaste on every cleanup path, including errors and panics, and warns not to assume terminal restoration covers modes the app enabled itself.
The answer recommends DEC private mode 2026 and wraps each frame in `ESC[?2026h` and `ESC[?2026l` so the terminal presents the completed frame at once.

It says Ratatui's diffing alone still lets changed cells appear progressively, and its code has the app call crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate and EndSynchronizedUpdate around `terminal.draw()` itself.
The code sends EndSynchronizedUpdate even when Begin or draw fails, and the answer adds it to panic cleanup and suspend. It warns that kitty can otherwise hold a stuck frame for about two seconds.
It detects support with DECRQM `ESC[?2026$p` under a bounded timeout and falls back when there is no reply or the mode is unsupported. It also advises redrawing only when state changes.
Recommends synchronized output (DEC mode 2026) and brackets each draw so the terminal presents the completed frame at once.
Says Ratatui's diffing does not make presentation atomic, and shows the app calling crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate/EndSynchronizedUpdate around terminal.draw itself.
Attempts EndSynchronizedUpdate even when draw errors, covers panic, shutdown and suspend paths, and notes terminal watchdog timeouts are only recovery mechanisms.
Describes probing with DECRQM (ESC[?2026$p) using a bounded timeout and falling back to ordinary rendering, and notes Ratatui emits only changed cells.
Recommends DEC private mode 2026, gives the begin and end sequences, and explains that the terminal holds the visible frame until the update ends.

Has the app bracket terminal.draw() with crossterm's BeginSynchronizedUpdate/EndSynchronizedUpdate itself and calls it a custom mode Ratatui's cleanup does not own, which implies Ratatui does not wrap draws automatically.
The code sends End even when Begin or draw fails, the answer covers panics and suspend, and it warns not to rely on kitty's roughly two-second watchdog.
Describes a timed DECRQM probe with reply parsing and falls back to buffered frame output, relying on Ratatui's changed-cell diffing on unsupported terminals.
Says legacy input encodes Enter and Shift+Enter as the same carriage-return byte (0x0d), and that the kitty protocol or modifyOtherKeys is needed to distinguish them.
Says Bubble Tea v2 enables kitty disambiguation and modifyOtherKeys, but the support must survive terminal → tmux, and tmux's extended-keys setting and version matter.
Makes Ctrl+J (0x0a) the always-available newline binding and treats Shift+Enter as an optional accelerator when it arrives distinctly.
Says to add Shift+Enter to the help when it is supported, keeping Ctrl+J in the footer; this ties the hints to detected support, though it does not name the reported enhancement message.
The answer says legacy input sends carriage return (0x0D) for both Enter and Shift+Enter, so the modifier is lost, and that kitty's keyboard protocol preserves it.
The answer says Bubble Tea v2 negotiates enhanced keyboard input, but legacy terminals lose the modifier and tmux extended keys are commonly disabled, needing `set -s extended-keys on`.
The answer makes Ctrl+J (LF 0x0A) the always-available newline binding and explicitly calls Shift+Enter an optional accelerator.

The answer says to advertise Shift+Enter only 'when the input path supports it' but never ties the hint to the terminal's enhanced-keyboard report, and it argues negotiation alone is insufficient evidence.
The answer says legacy input encodes both Enter and Shift+Enter as the same carriage-return byte, and that kitty's protocol (and modifyOtherKeys) preserves the distinction.
The answer says Bubble Tea v2 enables keyboard disambiguation but the whole input path must cooperate, and tmux needs `extended-keys on`, so otherwise modified keys don't survive.
The answer makes Ctrl+J the always-available newline binding and treats Shift+Enter as an optional shortcut used when distinguishable.
The answer keeps a stable fallback hint and adds Shift+Enter to the help only once support is established through capability queries.

The answer says to render immediately with a fallback palette and to query OSC 11 asynchronously through the event loop, accepting late replies.
The answer uses DA1 or CSI 5 n as a sentinel and enforces a 500 ms deadline, noting that some terminals never answer.

The answer says to emit `\x1b[0 q` (DECSCUSR reset) on every exit path, including normal quit, errors, and panics, and notes that Ratatui's restore() does not reset the cursor shape.
The answer says the previous shape cannot be reliably queried and that older xterm treats the reset as a blinking block.
